cross_system.title: Cross-system signal: credit card flow leading stock — origination headroom
cross_system.body: Credit card spending at ATMs grew 2.92%, e-commerce transactions rose 7.21%, and point-of-sale purchases increased 7.62% over the past year. Meanwhile, the actual credit card loan book grew only 2.29%. Spending is running ahead of the outstanding balance, which means people are using their cards more but the total amount they owe is growing more slowly.
cross_system.implication: Card users are transacting more but not carrying higher balances, which suggests either faster repayment or lower utilisation — both point to headroom for lenders to grow the book if they can encourage customers to borrow more or revolve balances.
chain: Card spending across channels is growing faster than the outstanding loan book
This gap means customers are using cards but paying down balances quickly or not maxing out limits
Lenders have room to grow the book by increasing credit limits or encouraging revolving credit

basis.headline: Credit card spend (value) (Payments) → Credit Card Outstanding (Credit): moving together
chain: Leading side: Credit card spend (value) (Payments) atm +2.9% · ecom +7.2% · other +270.4% · pos +7.6% YoY.
Lagging side: Credit Card Outstanding (Credit) +2.3% YoY.
The two sides are moving together → this reads as origination headroom.

cross_system.title: Unsecured retail credit appetite — expanding (5/5 measurements observed)
cross_system.body: Personal loans for credit cards and other purposes grew 2.3% and 14.7% year-on-year, while consumer durable loans rose 0.4%. Credit card outstanding balances are up 9.9% from last year. All four measures are moving in the same direction — upward — which means people are borrowing more for everyday spending and purchases without putting up collateral.
cross_system.implication: Unsecured retail lending is expanding across multiple categories at once, which is notable because it shows broad-based appetite for consumption credit rather than isolated strength in one product.
chain: People are taking more personal loans and using credit cards more heavily, with balances rising across the board
This happens when consumers feel confident enough to spend on credit without backing it with assets
Broad expansion across all unsecured categories signals widespread demand, making it a meaningful trend rather than a one-off spike in a single product

basis.headline: Unsecured retail credit appetite → expanding
basis.coverage: 5/5 measurements observed · all pulling the same way · Payments @ 2026-07-31 · Credit @ 2026-08-31
chain: Measured inputs: Credit Card Outstanding +2.3% YoY, Other Personal Loans +14.7% YoY, Consumer Durables +0.4% YoY, Credit card spend rising, Credit cards outstanding +9.9% YoY.
Member directions combine — measures and proxies count as-is, contra-indicators flipped — giving an expanding read on 5 of 5 measurements.
Those members are pulling the same way.

The willingness of households to carry — and lenders to extend — unsecured retail credit. No pipeline measures it directly: SIBC measures the unsecured stock (credit-card outstanding, other personal loans, consumer durables), payments measures the flow (credit-card spend) and reach (cards in force). Together they bound the construct: when stock, flow and reach move together the appetite read is unambiguous; when they diverge, the divergence itself is the signal.
Direction sustained across two composed periods → status active.

cross_system.title: Card-based consumption activity — expanding (5/5 measurements, contested)
cross_system.body: Card-based consumption activity is expanding, but the picture is mixed. Personal loans for consumer durables grew 0.39% year-on-year, and vehicle loans jumped 18.78%. At the same time, the number of card payment terminals fell 15.83%. The direction is a majority read — not all the numbers agree.
cross_system.implication: The growth in consumer-durable and vehicle lending is notable, but the drop in payment terminals suggests the expansion is uneven and may not be as broad-based as the loan numbers alone would imply.
chain: Loans for big-ticket items like durables and vehicles are growing, with vehicles up 18.78%
But the number of card terminals is down 15.83%, meaning fewer places accept card payments
The lending growth is real, yet the infrastructure for card-based spending is shrinking, so the expansion is patchy

basis.headline: Card-based consumption activity → expanding
basis.coverage: 5/5 measurements observed · but some members move against it · Payments @ 2026-07-31 · Credit @ 2026-08-31
chain: Measured inputs: Credit card spend rising, Debit card spend falling, POS terminals -15.8% YoY, Consumer Durables +0.4% YoY, Vehicle Loans +18.8% YoY.
Member directions combine — measures and proxies count as-is, contra-indicators flipped — giving an expanding read on 5 of 5 measurements.
Those members are NOT all pulling the same way — some move against the direction, so part of the movement cancels and the read rests on a majority rather than a consensus.

Household consumption as expressed through card rails. Payments measures the transaction flows (credit + debit card spend) directly; acceptance infrastructure (POS terminals) proxies the merchant side of the same activity; SIBC's consumer-durable and vehicle loan stocks proxy the credit-financed share of it.
Direction sustained across two composed periods → status active.

cross_system.title: Unsecured spend–stock cycle — running (3/3 segments live)
cross_system.body: This is a feedback cycle read across both pipelines: spending, balances, and appetite feed each other. The basis below shows each segment and whether it is currently running with the cycle or against it.
cross_system.implication: A fully-running cycle compounds; a segment moving against it is the early warning that the cycle is turning. Watch the reversed segment.
chain: Segment states: Unsecured retail credit appetite → Credit card spend (value) — running; Credit card spend (value) → Credit Card Outstanding — running; Credit Card Outstanding → Unsecured retail credit appetite — running.
A loop fires only when every segment runs in its expected direction; 3 of 3 are live, so the cycle is running.

Appetite expresses as card spend (flow), spend accumulates into card balances (stock), and growing balances evidence the appetite that started the cycle. The loop fires only when all three segments move the same way — a clean composed read that the unsecured retail cycle is running (or, reversed, unwinding). Segments span both pipelines plus the confirmed flow→stock cross-edge.

sibc.title: Co-lending & warehouse-financing infrastructure
sibc.body: Micro and small business lending jumped from 8.9% growth to 32.7% growth, an acceleration of 23.8pp. These loans now make up 22.8% of all MSME credit and are growing at 22.6% year-on-year. The gap between small-business loan growth and larger MSME loan growth is 4.9pp.
sibc.implication: Banks that set up co-lending partnerships and warehouse-financing arrangements with NBFCs can tap into fast-growing small-borrower volumes that their own branch networks struggle to reach efficiently.
chain: UDYAM registration and GST data make micro and small businesses easier to underwrite, so credit to them is accelerating sharply
Banks' own branches cannot cost-effectively originate thousands of small loans in every town and village
NBFCs that specialise in local origination need funding, so banks that provide warehouse lines or co-lend capture the volume without building expensive last-mile distribution
sibc._driver: MSME formalisation via UDYAM registration + GST data

sibc.title: Gold loan market entry / deepening for banks
sibc.body: Banks' gold loans grew 88.1% in the past year, and this growth has now continued for 16 straight periods. Banks are taking market share from NBFCs because they have branch networks that can test gold purity, store it safely, and handle cash — advantages that are hard to copy. Gold prices have surged since 2023, which means the same piece of gold now backs a bigger loan, so banks can lend more against it.
sibc.implication: The notable point for a lender is that this is not a short-term spike — 16 consecutive periods of growth signals that customers are shifting where they borrow against gold, and banks with physical branches have a lasting edge in capturing this business.
chain: Gold prices have risen sharply since 2023, so each gram of gold can now secure a larger loan than before
Banks with branch networks can test, store, and disburse gold loans on the spot, which NBFCs without branches struggle to match
This advantage has driven 88.1% year-on-year growth and sustained expansion for 16 periods in a row, showing customers are moving their gold-backed borrowing to banks

sibc.title: MSME origination infrastructure investment window
sibc.body: Micro and small business lending grew 22.6% year-on-year and now makes up 22.8% of all MSME credit. Growth accelerated by 23.8pp, jumping from 8.9% to 32.7%. Banks that built UDYAM-linked underwriting and GST-based cash flow tools between 2022 and 2024 are now lending to these smaller borrowers at scale.
sibc.implication: Banks without this origination infrastructure are falling behind in the fastest-growing segment of MSME lending, and the window to catch up is narrowing as early movers harvest returns from their systems.
chain: UDYAM registration and GST data made micro and small businesses easier to assess for credit
Banks that invested in systems to use this data can now underwrite borrowers they couldn't reach before
Those banks are capturing the 22.6% growth in this segment while others without the tools are missing out
sibc._driver: MSME formalisation via UDYAM registration + GST data

sibc.title: PLI anchor-supplier chain finance
sibc.body: Bank credit to basic metals is growing at 24.5%, to chemicals at 30.0%, and to engineering at 40.1%. These sectors are home to many PLI scheme recipients now building factories and buying equipment. As these anchor companies ramp up, their suppliers—often smaller firms—need working capital to deliver parts, materials, and services on time.
sibc.implication: Supply chain finance tied to these PLI anchors is notable because the repayment comes from a large, creditworthy buyer rather than the small supplier alone, lowering the lender's risk compared to a standalone loan to the same small firm.
chain: PLI companies in metals, chemicals, and engineering are drawing down capital and placing large orders with suppliers
Suppliers need cash to fulfill those orders but may lack strong standalone credit profiles
Lenders can finance the supplier against the anchor's purchase order or invoice, so repayment flows from the anchor, not the supplier

sibc.title: PSLC market depth from PSL reclassification surplus
sibc.body: In October 2024 the RBI raised the ceiling for housing loans that count toward Priority Sector Lending targets. Banks that already had many loans just below the old ceiling suddenly saw those loans reclassified as PSL-eligible, giving them a surplus. Banks with a surplus can sell PSL Certificates to banks that are short on their targets. Housing loan growth under PSL rules is running at 10.6% year-on-year, so the pool of tradable certificates has expanded.
sibc.implication: A one-time reclassification has created a deeper secondary market for PSL Certificates, meaning banks with surplus PSL credit can monetise it by selling to banks that need to meet targets, and banks short on PSL now have more supply to buy from.
chain: The RBI raised the housing loan ceiling for PSL eligibility in October 2024, so loans that were previously too large to count now qualify.
Banks holding many of these loans saw an instant reclassification surplus without making new loans.
Banks with surplus can sell PSL Certificates to banks falling short, expanding the secondary market and creating a monetisation opportunity.
sibc._driver: RBI PSL housing loan ceiling revision (Oct 2024)

sibc.title: Renewable energy project finance — next capex wave
sibc.body: Traditional infrastructure lending is slowing — some segments are down 31.6% year-on-year, others falling 13.2% or 0.8%. Meanwhile, renewable energy project lending is growing 58.4% and 21.6% in key categories. Banks that built project finance teams for roads and power over the past few years now have a new pipeline: solar, wind, and green hydrogen projects backed by government targets.
sibc.implication: Lenders with infrastructure project finance experience can shift that capability to renewable energy deals, where growth is running at 58.4% while older infrastructure segments are shrinking.
chain: Traditional infrastructure projects (roads, conventional power) are maturing and repaying loans, so those loan books are shrinking.
Government renewable energy targets are creating a large new pipeline of solar, wind, and hydrogen projects that need financing.
Banks that already know how to evaluate and finance big infrastructure projects can use the same skills on renewable deals, capturing growth in a new but similar market.
sibc._via: Project lifecycle phase → new origination vs repayment

sibc.title: Services sector credit entry / scale-up
sibc.body: Services sector credit is growing at 22.9%, much faster than other sectors, and has picked up speed by 7.0pp in the past year (from 12.0% to 19.0%). Within services, NBFC lending is surging at 79.5% year-on-year, and commercial real estate credit is up 43.3%. Services now makes up 28.2% of all bank credit.
sibc.implication: A lender without a services book — especially NBFC and commercial real estate — is missing the fastest-growing part of the credit market, which is pulling ahead by several percentage points every year.
chain: Services credit is growing at 22.9%, well above the overall credit market, and accelerating.
Within services, NBFC lending (79.5% growth) and commercial real estate (43.3% growth) are the main drivers.
Lenders focused elsewhere are under-represented in the segment that is expanding fastest and taking a bigger share of total credit.
sibc._driver: Bank→NBFC risk weights restored to external-rating basis (RBI, eff. 1 Apr 2025)

sibc.title: EV-specific vehicle credit products
sibc.body: RETIRED at first FOUNDATION (2026-06-10). No external source verified for EV share of vehicle loans or EV-specific credit risk differentiation. No L1 signal separating EV from ICE vehicle loans. Returns only when EV share of vehicle loans is measurable in L1 (e.g., VAHAN registration data ingestion).

sibc.title: Infrastructure repayment wave with insufficient new origination pipeline
sibc.body: Banks over-indexed to traditional infrastructure credit face a structural squeeze: the FY22-24 project book moves to repayment (compressing balances) while the next-cycle pipeline (renewables, data centres) is slower to ramp. Banks without next-cycle project finance capability face credit portfolio contraction.
chain: As a project cohort moves from construction (drawdown) to operations (repayment), net credit balance declines unless new origination offsets it — suppressing growth even while existing books remain large.
This is being driven by Infrastructure supercycle completing (FY22–24).
sibc._via: Project lifecycle phase → new origination vs repayment

sibc.title: CIC reporting compliance gaps creating off-balance-sheet credit risk
sibc.body: RBI Digital Lending Guidelines (2022/2025) require BNPL and digital credit to report to Credit Information Companies. However, compliance may be incomplete among newer digital lenders operating under first-loss guarantee structures or co-lending arrangements where the regulated entity's on-book exposure is partially shielded. If reporting gaps exist, the true unsecured credit stress is understated in bank balance sheets and in SIBC data.
chain: Higher risk weights raise the regulatory capital cost per unit of exposure, compressing origination economics for unsecured retail products until reversed.
This is being driven by RBI risk-weight hike on unsecured credit (Nov 2023).
sibc._driver: RBI risk-weight hike on unsecured credit (Nov 2023)
sibc._via: Regulatory capital weight → unsecured origination economics

atm_pos.title: Credit card penetration deepening — PSB share gap is the opening
atm_pos.body: Public sector banks hold 23.9% of all credit cards but 64% of debit cards — a gap of roughly 40 percentage points. Private banks hold 70.7% of credit cards. Total credit cards outstanding are 12.3 crore and growing at 9.9% year-on-year. The biggest recent gains came from private banks (1.1 crore new cards) while public sector banks lost 2.9 lakh cards.
atm_pos.implication: Public sector banks have a large pool of existing debit card customers who do not yet have credit cards, and converting these customers costs less than finding entirely new ones — so the gap is an opening for lenders who can reach those customers.
chain: Public sector banks serve most debit card holders but issue far fewer credit cards than private banks
Upgrading an existing customer from debit to credit card is cheaper than acquiring a stranger
The 40-point share gap means millions of potential credit card customers are already banked but underserved

atm_pos.title: Rural cash distribution via Micro ATM / Business Correspondent networks
atm_pos.body: India has 13.3 lakh micro ATMs, down -9.4% from last year. These are small cash-dispensing devices run by local agents in villages and small towns. Even as the overall ATM network shrinks, micro ATMs remain at over 13 lakh units because many rural areas still need cash but cannot support the cost of a full ATM or bank branch.
atm_pos.implication: The 13.3 lakh micro ATM base, despite a -9.4% decline, shows that rural cash demand persists at a level where low-cost agent networks are more viable than building full infrastructure — notable for lenders who want rural reach without heavy branch investment.
chain: Rural areas need cash access but full ATMs and branches cost too much to run there
Micro ATMs let local agents handle cash at much lower cost so over 13 lakh are still operating
Lenders can reach these customers by partnering with agent networks instead of building their own branches

atm_pos.title: Embedded transit and tap-to-pay payment products
atm_pos.body: Credit card spending in the 'other' category jumped 270.4% by value and 142.2% by volume in the past year. This category includes transit tap-to-pay and embedded payment products that let people use cards in new everyday situations — buses, metros, and UPI-linked credit transactions. The value is growing much faster than the number of transactions, which means people are using these new payment methods for bigger purchases once they get comfortable with them.
atm_pos.implication: A new everyday use case for credit cards is taking hold quickly, and the gap between value growth (270.4%) and volume growth (142.2%) shows that early adopters are increasing how much they spend through these channels, not just how often.
chain: New payment infrastructure (transit NFC, UPI-linked credit) makes it possible to use credit cards in places that previously only took cash or debit
People try the new method for small purchases first, then use it for larger amounts as they get comfortable
Value grows faster than volume because each user is spending more per transaction over time, signaling the behaviour is sticking
atm_pos._driver: Embedded card payment infrastructure rollout (transit NFC or RuPay-credit-on-UPI)
atm_pos._via: Embedded payment rails → new card-spend surface

atm_pos.title: Credit card market concentrated in top-5 private banks
atm_pos.body: The top-5 private banks control approximately 71% of credit card outstanding. The largest single issuer holds ~20% of the market. This concentration creates systemic fragility — as demonstrated when a single payment bank's exit caused a market-wide debit card step-down. Similar disruption from a major credit card issuer would have proportionally larger effects.

atm_pos.title: Debit card base structural decline reducing cash access for underbanked
atm_pos.body: The debit card base is contracting through payment bank exits and lifecycle purges. This reduces the potential transaction base for populations that depend on debit cards for cash access and digital payments — particularly lower-income and rural segments without credit cards or reliable UPI-linked accounts.
chain: Regulatory wind-down of a major issuer forces cancellation of its entire card portfolio, producing a single-period step-down in the stock concentrated in that issuer's lender category.
This is being driven by RBI enforcement action against Paytm Payments Bank (deposits/top-ups barred after 15 Mar 2024).
atm_pos._driver: RBI enforcement action against Paytm Payments Bank (deposits/top-ups barred after 15 Mar 2024)

atm_pos.title: Payment acceptance bifurcation: POS contracting while UPI grows
atm_pos.body: POS terminal network contraction while UPI QR expands creates an acceptance gap: merchants who drop POS terminals cannot accept international cards, EMI transactions, premium credit card features, or POS-authenticated payments. Customers without UPI-linked accounts face reduced options at merchants who have switched fully to UPI.
chain: Zero MDR on UPI makes QR acceptance structurally cheaper than card POS (no hardware, no per-txn fee), driving QR deployment while suppressing POS-terminal investment. Polarity is per-target: + for QR, − for POS.
This is being driven by Zero MDR policy on UPI transactions (NPCI/GoI).
atm_pos._driver: Zero MDR policy on UPI transactions (NPCI/GoI)
